title: Perfume begins as smoke
text: In Mesopotamia and Egypt, resins and woods are burned for the gods. The word perfume comes from Latin 'per fumum', meaning 'through smoke'.

title: The oldest perfume workshop
text: Archaeologists found a Bronze Age perfume factory at Pyrgos in Cyprus, with stills and jars that once held scents of pine, coriander, parsley and almond.

title: Hatshepsut's incense expedition
text: Queen Hatshepsut of Egypt sends ships to the land of Punt to bring back living frankincense and myrrh trees for her temple.

title: Tapputi, the first named perfumer
text: A Babylonian clay tablet names Tapputi, a woman who made perfumes for the royal palace by distilling flowers, oil and calamus with water. She is the first chemist whose name we know.

title: Rome falls in love with scent
text: Romans perfume their baths, clothes and even horses. Pliny the Elder describes dozens of perfume recipes in his Natural History.

title: Avicenna and rose water
text: Rose water was already being distilled in the Islamic world, but the Persian physician Ibn Sina (Avicenna) improved the method and wrote it down, helping open the way to essential oils.

title: Hungary Water
text: One of the first alcohol-based perfumes, made mostly of rosemary, is said to have been created for a queen of Hungary.

title: Catherine de' Medici brings perfume to France
text: Catherine de' Medici marries the future King Henry II and brings her perfumer, René le Florentin, to Paris. Perfumed gloves become the fashion.

title: The glovers-perfumers of Grasse and Paris
text: French glove makers win the right to call themselves perfumers. Grasse, a tanning town, starts growing flowers to scent its leather and becomes the perfume capital.

title: Eau de Cologne is born
text: Giovanni Maria Farina, an Italian living in Cologne, creates a light citrus water he names after his new city. Napoleon is said to have ordered it by the crate.

title: The first Paris perfume houses
text: Jean-François Houbigant opens his shop in Paris. Guerlain follows in 1828, and Paris becomes the home of luxury perfume.

title: The first synthetic scent molecule
text: William Henry Perkin makes coumarin, the sweet smell of hay and tonka bean, in the lab. Perfumers can now use smells that nature can't give them.

title: Vanillin is made in the lab
text: German chemists Ferdinand Tiemann and Wilhelm Haarmann synthesise vanillin, making vanilla affordable for everyone.

title: Fougère Royale
text: Paul Parquet for Houbigant mixes lavender, oakmoss and synthetic coumarin. It creates the fougère family, still the base of many men's perfumes.

title: Jicky
text: Aimé Guerlain's Jicky is one of the first perfumes to use synthetics boldly, and one of the oldest still on sale.

title: Ionones: violets for all
text: Chemists Tiemann and Krüger discover ionones, the smell of violets. Violet perfumes become a Belle Époque craze.

title: Coty's Chypre
text: François Coty pairs bergamot, oakmoss and labdanum. Chypre gives its name to a whole perfume family.

title: Chanel No 5
text: Ernest Beaux creates No 5 for Coco Chanel with an overdose of aldehydes. It becomes the world's most famous perfume.

title: Shalimar
text: Jacques Guerlain's Shalimar, rich in vanilla and resins, sets the template for the 'oriental' (amber) family.

title: Vent Vert
text: Germaine Cellier, one of the first famous women perfumers, uses a record dose of galbanum in Balmain's Vent Vert, the first big 'green' perfume.

title: Ambrox replaces ambergris
text: Firmenich creates Ambrox, a lab-made version of the key smell in ambergris - a rare, costly material that washes up on beaches from sperm whales.

title: Eau Sauvage and the radiance of Hedione
text: Edmond Roudnitska's Eau Sauvage for Dior is the first big perfume to use Hedione, an airy jasmine molecule that makes scents glow.

title: Iso E Super
text: IFF chemists discover Iso E Super, a velvety, skin-like wood that changes the way modern perfumes smell.

title: The powerhouse decade
text: Dior's Poison leads a wave of loud, long-lasting perfumes that fill a room, the signature of the 1980s.

title: The sea arrives
text: Davidoff Cool Water and Aramis New West use Calone, a watery molecule, to launch the fresh 'aquatic' family of the 1990s.

title: Angel and the gourmands
text: Thierry Mugler's Angel smells of candy floss and chocolate. It creates the 'gourmand' family of edible-smelling perfumes.

title: CK One: one scent for everyone
text: Calvin Klein's CK One is marketed for everyone, making unisex perfume mainstream.

title: The rise of niche perfume
text: Frédéric Malle launches Editions de Parfums, putting the perfumer's name on the bottle. Independent 'niche' houses boom.

title: Oud goes west
text: Yves Saint Laurent's M7 introduces oud to Western perfumery. A decade later, oud is everywhere.

title: A perfume made of one molecule
text: Escentric Molecules' Molecule 01 is pure Iso E Super, a cult hit that shows how powerful a single molecule can be.

title: The Ambroxan era
text: Dior's Sauvage, built on Ambroxan, becomes one of the best-selling perfumes ever and defines the 2010s.

title: Biotech and cleaner molecules
text: Perfumers turn to fermentation and 'upcycled' materials, while the EU bans some classic molecules such as Lilial (2022) over safety concerns.
